slides.headline: Critics said this title was wrong
London, 1886
slides.text: Watts paints a lone woman sitting on top of the world, and calls it Hope. But critics looked closer and saw something else.

slides.headline: She can't see
slides.text: Look at her face first: a blindfold. Head bowed, she sits alone, with no idea where she is going.

slides.headline: Broken strings
slides.text: And her lyre? Every string has snapped except one. She presses her ear against it, straining to hear what is left.

slides.headline: "Call it Despair"
slides.text: No wonder several critics said it should have been called Despair. One called it a ghastly and apocalyptic allegory. So why Hope?

slides.headline: The last string
slides.text: Watts answered simply: "Hope need not mean expectancy. It suggests here rather the music which can come from the remaining chord."

slides.headline: Look up
slides.text: And there is one more clue she cannot see: a single small star above her head. Decades later, preachers started noticing it too.

slides.headline: From canvas to pulpit
slides.text: In 1959, Martin Luther King preached on it. Around 1990, Jeremiah Wright built a sermon on it: The Audacity to Hope.

slides.headline: One string, one president
slides.text: In the pews sat Barack Obama. His 2006 book became The Audacity of Hope. So, do you see hope here, or despair?
